name: Append-Only Data
subject: blockchain
subjectTitle: Blockchain: A Skeptic's Guide to Trust Technologies

lesson.title: Adding to the Record Without Rewriting It
lesson.summary: Append-only data structures allow new entries to be added to the end of a record but forbid changing or removing anything already written, which is what makes a blockchain's immutability enforceable in practice.
lesson.body:
Immutability describes a goal: past data should not change undetected. Append-only is the design rule that actually achieves it. An append-only structure is one where the only permitted operation on existing data is adding new data after it. You cannot edit entry number 500 once entries 501 through 900 have been written on top of it, and you cannot delete entry 500 either. The only way forward is forward.

This is a much older idea than blockchain. Accountants have long used bound ledger books for exactly this reason: a mistake could not be erased, only corrected with a new, dated entry that explicitly reverses or adjusts the old one, leaving a visible trail of both the error and its correction. Write ahead logs in traditional databases work the same way, recording every change as a new entry rather than overwriting old state, so the database can always be reconstructed by replaying the log from the start. Blockchain did not invent append-only design, it applied a very old bookkeeping principle to a cryptographically verified, distributed setting where thousands of separate parties, not one bookkeeper, are watching the ledger for exactly this kind of tampering.

The connection to immutability is direct and mechanical. Because each new block's hash depends on the previous block's hash, the structure is naturally append-only: adding a new block at the end is cheap and normal, but going back and modifying an old block breaks the hash chain in the way described in the previous section. Append-only is the shape of the data structure; immutability is the security property that shape produces once the ledger is also distributed and replicated across many nodes.

A practical example makes the distinction between "append-only" and "unchangeable meaning" clearer. Suppose a smart contract on a blockchain records that a user's account balance is 100 tokens, and later a transaction spends 30 of them. The record of the original 100 is never erased or edited, it remains on the chain forever. What happens instead is that a new entry is appended recording the spend, and any program reading the chain calculates the current balance, 70 tokens, by processing the full append-only history from the start. Correcting an error works the same way: you do not unwrite the mistake, you append a correcting transaction, exactly like the accountant crossing out an entry with a single line and writing the correction below it, dated and signed.

The tradeoff is that an append-only ledger only ever grows. There is no built-in way to shrink it, compress away old irrelevant history, or forget data that should legally be forgotten, which becomes a genuine tension with regulations like the right to erasure in data protection law. Append-only gives you a trustworthy, tamper-evident history at the cost of a record that never gets smaller and, in a sense, never lets go.
